title: The Wave That Climbed Higher Than a Skyscraper
disclosure: This episode recounts the verified 1958 Lituya Bay megatsunami; stock footage is representational coverage, not literal footage of the event.

story.person: Howard Ulrich, a fisherman and father aboard the Edrie
story.central_question: How can a quiet bay throw water higher than a skyscraper, and what does survival look like from inside the wave?
story.risk: If the Edrie cannot break free before the surge arrives, Howard and his son will be carried into the shore.
story.irreversible_decision: Howard pays out the anchor chain and starts the engine instead of waiting for the wave to hit.
story.consequence: The Edrie is lifted, carried toward shore and pulled back by the backwash; Howard and his son survive.

story.something_to_lose: His son's life and the ability to leave the bay together.
story.hook: Howard is asleep beside his seven-year-old son when the mountain above Lituya Bay begins to move.
story.reveal: The highest recorded tsunami run-up began not in the open ocean, but when a mountainside entered a narrow inlet.

beats.text: Howard Ulrich was asleep in a small boat in Alaska's Lituya Bay
when the mountain above his seven-year-old son began to move. On July ninth, nineteen fifty-eight,
a magnitude seven point nine earthquake tore the shoreline open. Howard woke to the sound
of rock and ice collapsing into Gilbert Inlet. The impact did not make an ordinary wave.
It threw water up the opposite slope, one thousand seven hundred and twenty feet—higher than the Empire State Building.
The surge stripped the forest and carried debris across the land.
Howard could not free the anchor. He paid out the chain—started the engine—and waited.
The Edrie rose with the wall of water and was carried toward shore.
Then the backwash pulled the boat away.
Another boat sank near the entrance. Two men died.
Howard and his son survived, but the forest kept the evidence: a clean scar thousands of feet above the tide.
Lituya Bay proved a tsunami does not need an ocean. Sometimes a mountain is enough.

idea.title: The Wave That Climbed Higher Than a Skyscraper
idea.premise: In 1958, Howard Ulrich and his seven-year-old son survived as a landslide in Alaska's Lituya Bay launched water 1,720 feet up a mountainside.
idea.audience_promise: Follow one father's seconds-long fight to keep a small boat alive inside the highest tsunami run-up ever recorded.
idea.central_question: How can a quiet bay throw water higher than a skyscraper, and what does survival look like from inside the wave?

truth.disclosure: This episode recounts the verified 1958 Lituya Bay megatsunami; stock footage is representational coverage, not literal footage of the event.
truth.reconstruction_note: The event is historical; the visual clips are rights-documented representational footage and historical public-domain evidence.
